txt: A loud sigh comes through the headphones. "Be advised, officer. The signal is liable to fail any moment now..."
A strange woman makes straight for the radiocomputer.
And then nothing.

In the silence, a low hum starts creeping up your spine. It's a song inside you -- not in the speakers, not in the room. A great bass sigh in the basement of your mind. Slowly it builds, until the air around you starts to vibrate.
Nothing happens as Soona Luukanen-Kilde presses unmute on her keyboard. Nothing but silence.
She doesn't answer, her eyes closed and brows knitted together in a state of deep focus, one hand cupping the headphone.
She doesn't talk, her eyes closed and brows knitted together in a state of deep focus, one hand cupping the headphone.
She falls silent. The wind blows in through the hole in the stained glass window. Cold and moist.
She gets back to work.
She has already turned back to her keyboard.
She inhales sharply, before answering in a single breath: "Because I needed something *good* for my investigation and Rehm Civic is widely agreed to be below all standards, so I had to upgrade."
She looks up from her monitor. "You're asking me to circuit-bend onto Coalition radio frequencies. You want to know is it possible? Probably. But is it a good idea? I'm not so sure..."
She looks up into the darkness under the nave, then back at you.

She pats her glowing machine. "Prefect is mainly based on the same technology as Rehm Civic, so it's kind of a rip-off, but it does have better compatibility with newer antenna models, so I won't complain."
She pauses, looking you in the eye.
She shrugs and turns back to her radiocomputer.
She shrugs. "One more thing -- maybe a club for anodic music isn't the *worst* thing you can erect around this particular... *point in space*?"
She shrugs. "You know -- maybe a club for anodic music isn't the *worst* thing you can erect around this particular... *point in space*?"
She sighs. "I'm afraid we're out of alternatives. You're just going to have to *go for it*."
She stares at the terminal, completely oblivious to her surroundings.
She starts laughing, but stops almost immediately, her voice oddly humourless: "No, it's not dangerous, just depressing."
She thinks about it, a glassy look in her eyes. A gust of wind brings more snow in from the broken gallery. It touches her hair.
She turns off her computer and leaves.
She's silent for a second. Then she opens her mouth. "According to this -- how long..."
She's still typing behind the radiocomputer, her sweater-clad frame hunched over the machine.
Soona doesn't reply, her hands running over the printout. She's looking for something -- for her morning star -- eyes scouring the millimetres.
The lead programmer sends you an encouraging thumbs up from across the hall.
The lead programmer sighs. "I can't believe they got you so easily. Go have another talk with those up-and-coming entrepreneurs, will you? Thanks."
The lead programmer throws the other young woman a knowing glance before turning her attention back to her own work.
The lead programmer turns to look at you for a moment, her gaze impassive, then returns to her work.
The paper gets soaked in ink again, its evil blackness shining in the light of the mainframe. It looks eerie.
The paper starts filling out with ink, soaking it in a gleaming blackness. Not a single line of data stands out.
The paper starts filling out with ink, soaking it in a gleaming darkness. Not a single line of data stands out.
The programmer eyes you curiously. She does not understand why you're hesitating.
The programmer gives you an impatient look before returning to her radiocomputer.
The programmer seems to consider the question for a moment, then dismisses it with a flick of her wrist...
The woman looks around. In the silence, you see dust move on the floorboards. The driver of the speaker vibrates in the air and then stops. Plasterwork begins to crumble down the walls...
You're so engrossed in your reading that you don't even notice the sound of the door opening...
"*And what is it doing in the fridge?!*"
"*Ghosts?*" she repeats. "No, I don't think so, I don't believe in ghosts."
"... equals equals false, close brackets, equals equals true?"
"... not the worst idea..."
"...are astronomically low."
"A better sound system?" she repeats. "Alright... But where would we get one?"
"A chance to cook some speed, you mean?" she asks sourly, crossing her arms.
"A speck of white?" She sounds excited, as the filament clicks into place. "That's exactly what I'm hoping to find."
"Absolutely not. My Rehm Prefect is my livelihood. If something were to go wrong, it would be a disaster."
"Acele, aren't you going to dance?"
"Again."
"Ah! Very good thinking. I'll engage it now..."
"Ah, but there *is* and it *protects* me!"
"Ah, very good. Let's see what you have."
"Ah, yes. I wasn't sure what to do about that, but then I discovered an abandoned power source down by the edge of the bay."
"Ah, you 'found' the transceiver from my old Rehm Civic. Did you think I wouldn't recognise it? No matter. It should work for our purposes..."
"Ah. Very good, officer."
"Ah. Yes, I did notice that it was covered in police livery. Then you already know that the carriage itself is irreparable, but the rear-mounted engine seems to be in fine working order..."
"Aha, excellent! You are connected. Now be quick, I don't know how long I'll be able to preserve the signal."
"Alright, this is all very good and sad, but I have my research to finish. Trust me, this is far more important than the fate of some local speedfreaks and their dance music."
"Alright, well... All radiocomputers perform operations up on air, so in order to gain more processing power you need to invest in a *good antenna*."

"Alright," she finally says, blinking twice. "Bring me the game's off-site copy from my old workspace if you really want to help. It's stored on a filament memory and I'm unable to go and fetch it myself."
"And I don't have a..." She stops mid-sentence. "You know what, it would be really helpful if you could just stop talking and let me work."
"And before you go on, I am *not* disrupting any order here, I'm a circuit bender and no one has anything against circuit benders."
"And here's my Kvalsund multitool. You might need it to hack loose some ice. It opens everything. If you get me the off-site copy, then you can keep the Kvalsund."

"And information," she nods. "Causing data losses in the East-Insulindian front. Have you considered why it's formed in a church? And, also, *when* or *how* it might start growing? Or -- if it has other effects? In addition to sound and data..."

"And no, taking it outside the building *wouldn't* have protected it from the data loss. There's nothing wrong with keeping the backup in the basement. What happened was a freak accident that has nothing to do with how the backup was stored."
"And now if you'll just connect that here..."
"And the Heads -- I won't even get *into* the Heads, millions of them..." She stops. "Go find that copy from that ice cream maker, will you? Thanks."
"And we're also unlikely to change our local entroponetic conditions. So the next step is to thoroughly inspect our connections."
"And?"
"Anytime." She smiles.
"Anyway..." She turns back to her terminal. "You should do some research before you decide to buy anything. Ask around, compare the prices. There are many milieus dedicated to that sort of thing."
"Archer can't hear us, I'm afraid. Only his microphone is connected to the transceiver."
"Are you alright, officer?"
"Assuming the relay isn't too badly damaged, that is. I have work to do here, but I recommend you examine the relay tower and return once you have determined its condition."
"Because I'm afraid that something might happen. It's an unknown phenomenon..." She turns to Egg Head. "We can always turn it back up if there's a need."
"Because it reminds us of death. And we humans tend to think that death is pretty scary."
"Because it's a completely different class of antenna. It would be like using a high-end racing carriage where a long-distance lorry is required."
"Because it's just trial and error, trying to locate the swallow -- the exact point in space."
"Because she's from Martinaise and people from Martinaise have never ever seen a radiocomputer. She thinks it emits elemental *evil*."
"Besides, owning a Rehm Prefect isn't such a big deal anymore."
"Bingo." She snaps her fingers. "That's exactly what they're up to."
"Breaking into my radiocomputer again, I see." She glares at you as she holds down the OFF button for several seconds. The machine reboots.
"Breaking into my radiocomputer, I see." She glares at you as she holds down the OFF button for several seconds. The machine reboots.
"But honestly, it's not progressing very well." She grows silent, staring at her circle of basins -- it looks like some ancient ritual.
"But it *is*, because *you* broke it."
"But it's not the cheapest one on the market, so I wouldn't recommend it for your regular red tape operations. Fraser 1000 is a foolproof line for civilians."
"But most of the time I'm fully absorbed in my work with the radiocomputer," she then goes on, "and there are still parts of the church I haven't had time to explore, so..."
"But the gradient -- it clearly hasn't started yet. We're here and the pale is not."
"But the milk -- it clearly hasn't started curdling yet. We're here and the pale is not."

"But this..." She raises her head, staring at all the machines that litter the church, cables coiling up on the floor like pests. "This is just another failure. Silence sounds like silence. That's all it is."
"But you didn't, you made things worse."
"But..." She looks up, and there's fear in her eyes as she considers the possibility. "But pale isn't here. We're thousands of kilometres from the edge."
"Can you please just go and move the water bowls for me? Thanks."
"Certainly, though it requires a fair amount of technical finesse to remove them. Frankly, it's not worth the bother. Just find a regular radio."
"Come on, that's..." She was about to dismiss your latest idea out of hand, but something gives her pause.
"Could you..." She closes her eyes. "Could you just... *shh* for a moment? Or get to the point -- I really need to focus on something."
"Damn it! I'm going to push the power supply. I doubt it will last more than a few minutes, so you'd better make them count."
"Damn, I was afraid of that. And I didn't bring any solvents with me. How foolish..."
"Damn..." The programmer removes her sweat-drenched headphones. "Even with the crosstalk suppressed the signal is still very weak."
"Damnit." She lets out a loud sigh, before tearing off her headphones; she's still avoiding your gaze.
"Do I look like someone who has time for *side projects* at this moment?" She doesn't even look up from her computer.
"Do you have access to a giant boat?"
"Don't worry, you can't miss the bear." She gives you a rueful smile. "It's hideous."
"Don't you think the Union would object to that?"
"Done!" Soona jumps up from the keyboard like a spring. "I've got it, I've found the location of the anomaly!" There's joy in her voice as she bumps her fist into air.
"EGG HEAD. A 3.5 CABLE!" She rises a black cable. "INTO THE AUXILIARY INPUT! OKAY?"
"Eh?" She frowns. "Come on, it's not about your brain -- even I couldn't figure it out on my own."

"Exactly, what *does* it mean?" There's something frantic about her as she locks her gaze with you, eyes shining like pearls. "Up to now it has been impossible to say what it is, because it's impossible to measure *nothing*."
"Exactly," she nods, "very true! That's what I've been aiming for, that's why I have those basins. I've tried using hydrotransducers to record the silence -- to find out where it *begins*."
"Figure it out?" She shakes her head, grinning. "No, I don't need you to figure anything out, I've got a computer for that." She pats the mainframe.
"Finally, there's the question of *stimulants*. Some people prefer to keep illegal amphetamines on-hand to help with their work. I am not one of them, but they do exist."
"Five..."
"Fortunately, we have a more-than-adequate transceiver, so I do not believe it is causing any problems..."
"Four years..." the woman whispers. "Twenty two people, millions of reáls... All that time *this* is what we were up against? Just erased it..." Her lip trembles. "Sulisław isn't gonna believe this."
"Four..."
"Go ahead, officer."
"God..." She immediately steps back and raises her hands, sensing the aggression. "Easy now, I'll go. It's not an issue. Can I pack my things first?"
"God..." The girl immediately steps back and raises her hands. "Easy now, I'll go, it's not an issue! Can I pack my things first?"
"Good -- then you might know the giant ice bear fridge in the building's cellar. The filament is inside the fridge -- just go and get it."
"Good. Beginning transmission."
"Good. Now, give me a hand with these amplifiers. Leave the cables. I don't feel like making two trips..."
"Good." She gets back to work.
"Good."
"Great, everything should be aligned now..." She stops, biting into her chapped lip.
"Great, someone got through to him. Okay, let's get it all set up. Can we turn the music off, please?"
"Great. What are we talking about? And *why*?" She gets back to work -- a clear signal that this branch of the conversation is over.
"Great." Her hands are a whirl on the keyboard. "Thanks."
"Great." She dwells back into the glowing terminal.
"Have some dignity," the woman sighs, turning back to her radiocomputer.
"He doesn't listen to me. He only ever seems to care about *hard core* and *Yekokataa*, 'a place to be' apparently."
"Here," she suddenly says, rising her ink-stained fingertip, "I found it."
"Hmm, I had hoped that between the signal purifier and cleaning the connections that we would have it, but perhaps I overestimated."
"Hmm, it seems to have made some difference, but unfortunately not enough to alter the overall situation."
"Hmm, what a disappointment. I was almost sure something *truly* interesting was about to happen. Oh well."
"Hmmm..."
"Hold on." She's behind the keyboard now, typing in some numbers that only she understands. The terminal beeps, and the light inside starts pulsing like a glowing heart.
"Honestly..." She's avoiding your gaze. "Honestly, I'm a little scared."
"Huh. The signal is coming through a bit clearer now. Good work."
"Huh?" She looks up, puzzled.
"I *am* being careful. Treat it as a mere technical anomaly, makes it easier to bear." She runs her hands over the printout, searching for something...
"I CAN'T HEAR YOU!" she shouts, pointing at the enormous speaker that's churning out the sound. "THE MUSIC IS TOO LOUD!"
"I already told you -- I'm not interested."
"I am Soona Luukanen-Kilde, the former lead programmer of Fortress Accident and RSA Radios. I have over 16 years of programming experience and I'm proficient in both Vox and Orbis languages..."
"I am conducting scientific research here. You can't throw me out," she says, ready to stand her ground.

"I believe that means we're ready to get started. I should warn you, once we begin setting up this antenna, we'll need to see the whole process through. There won't be any second chances, any 'do-overs,' you understand?"
"I believe you mean, what *was* he talking about."
"I brought them here. These are my machines. Please don't touch anything."
"I can't say with certainty, but it *sounds* very much like entroponetic crosstalk. It happens sometimes when sending transmissions across long stretches of pale."
"I cannot answer that for you, but I don't expect it to be *that* difficult. There's no shortage of radios around here."
"I did not expect simply locating the signal to be so difficult." She appears to be concentrating very intently.
"I didn't see anything. I was focussed on my work. Have you checked the connections yet, or no?"
"I do not think that the boss of the Union would like us using his equipment to contact the Coalition."
"I don't believe in them either."
"I don't care, I don't care about crab men." She barely looks up, now tinkering with the machine's printer.
"I don't care," she blurts, then reconsiders: "But thank you anyway."
"I don't know about your relationship to the Union, but I do not think they would appreciate us using their equipment to contact the Coalition."
"I don't know, I'm just scared. Maybe it's going to be something terrifying. Maybe it's going to tear the world apart."
"I don't know, are we? That's what I'm trying to figure out here. But how *do* I figure it out?"
"I don't know." She stares at the heart of her computer. "That's what I'm scared of: I don't know. It could be *anything*."
"I don't see any alternative. We're just going to have to build the antenna ourselves."
"I don't take them because they make me nauseous, but everyone has their reasons. I don't judge."
"I don't want to make anything work," she replies, her expression unchanged.
"I don't."
"I feel that's illegal."
"I found the coordinates!" She lets out a celebratory laugh.
"I guess I could live through a week or two of peaceful coexistence."
"I guess it is…" She stops to think. "So far I've been quite satisfied with it. Martinaise is an unstable region with bad coverage and the operation has been surprisingly stable."

"I have a theory," she says, as the filament clicks into place, "Lintel was able to divine the anomaly's location from this broken copy. I want to repeat their calculation, only this time with better equipment."

"I have a theory," she says, as the filament clicks into place. "Lintel was able to divine the location of the anomaly from this broken copy. I want to repeat their calculation, only this time with better equipment."
"I have considered the same. The bad news is -- there were *seven* pinewood churches built in the first decade of Revachol's settlement."
"I have no idea. I've never even heard of anything like this."
"I have plenty of cables and amplifiers on hand. The power supply I will secure on my own. All we require now is the radio transceiver itself."
"I highly doubt it. That tower is barely able to transmit short-wave signals across the bay. To generate mega-low frequencies, we're going to need a *much* larger antenna..."

"I know a friend of a friend who used to freelance for the Coalition," she says nonchalantly, scratching her ear. "I was actually aiming for the military-grade Rehm Rational series, but couldn't find one."

"I know it's just ink," she replies, as the filament clicks into place, "but Lintel was somehow able to divine the location of the anomaly from this broken copy. I want to repeat their calculation, only this time with better equipment."
"I know, I know it is, but... could you *please* turn it down just this instance? Just *this* one time -- maximum is *not* the only way, okay?"
"I know."
"I mean, what sound does the nothing make? How can you even listen to something that doesn't exist?" She turns to face you, the mainframe throwing shadows on her chin.
"I need you to go move those water bowls for me, I need to double-check my calculations."
"I promise, I promise!" she exclaims, words echoing below the ceiling rafters.
"I promise, officer. We will *not* play it again."
"I see you've talked to them, good. Drugs are illegal, and I'm not leaving this church -- especially because of some corrupt drug lab idea you've cooked up in that tent."
"I sincerely doubt that's the case, but there's nothing I can do about it from down here. I should've cleaned them beforehand. How foolish..."

"I told the producers we need to go and move to a normal office building, with amenities. But no -- the artists like the *milieu*. The writers like the *history*..." She shakes her head. "I told them."
"I told them, but no -- normal office buildings are *bourgeois*..."
"I understand..." She closes her eyes. "A theory of the pale where instead of an *outer ocean* it metastasises -- like a cancer or a mould -- erupting in points *inside* the world."
"I use the AR-1 as my Rehm Prefect's processing unit."
"I very much doubt anyone from the Wild Pines would allow us to turn their boat into a giant radio transmitter."

"I was actually aiming for the military-grade Rehm Rational series, but couldn't find one." She pats her machine: "Prefect is mainly based on the same technology as the Civic, but it does work better with newer antenna models, so I'm not complaining."
"I wouldn't go so far as to..."
"I'm a circuit bender and no one ever has anything against circuit benders."
"I'm going to leave that out -- but the rest... some of this I can use to *start* to explain this to the rest of the team. Maybe I'll sound mad, but..."
"I'm looking for the location of a two-millimetre hole in the world."
"I'm not interested in irony. I leave that to more *conceptual* types."
"I'm not joking, officer. I'll only be able to hold the signal open for a few more moments. What you came here to ask, ask it now..."
"I'm not sure how much longer I can keep the signal clear, officer."
"I'm protected by the Wayfarer Act."
"I'm still not certain whether this was a *good* idea or not, but there is something extraordinary about summoning an aerostatic with your voice..."
"I'm working."
"Ideally, narrow the receiving mode, so that we can isolate the warship's signal and eliminate the crosstalk. But if you don't know what you're doing of course you could just make it worse."
"If we've got the location right, we should then be able to hear whatever sound this anomaly makes."
"If you could bring me the off-site copy then it would help -- a lot."
"If you have reál to spare, you might even be able to *buy* one. But it doesn't really matter where it comes from, so long as it works."
"If you would like to apologise, that is your business. I am only here to tell you what's feasible or not from a technical viewpoint."
"If you'll please carry that amplifier and cables, officer. We have quite a lot to carry..."
"If you're desperate for collaborators now, I suggest you ask your new friends. They seem to have plenty of time for side projects."
"If you're not here to hire me, I don't really know how can I help you." She turns back to the terminal.
"In any event, just leave that equipment here. I'll put it away later. If you'd like, you can take one of the extra headsets. I don't need so many spares."
"In that case, let's move on."
"In the giant ice bear fridge -- I just told you. It has red glowing eyes, it's impossible to miss. You just need to get the off-site copy from the ice bear."
"In the meantime, I will gather the rest of the materials. We will meet back here when you have it."
"In the meantime, you must keep trying."

"Interesting," she says as examines the transceiver, "an Esterhaz EH-4, heavily customised. This is an advanced model, highly capable. I'll need to replace the frequency dial, but it should certainly work for our purposes."

"Is this... a Kristallsprach?" She looks up at you as she gently opens the case. "The Model 9 is an excellent piece of equipment. I don't know what you had to pay for it, but it should work very nicely."
"It did look like you... short-circuited," she says, flipping through printouts.
"It doesn't *emit*, it receives..." She stops explaining. "You sound just like her. She started praying when she first saw my Rehm. Turned to higher powers."
"It is possible that technical fields attract a certain kind of personality. I haven't given it much thought."
"It isn't gibberish, it's Walder. Now please, keep trying."
"It must be entroponetic crosstalk. The one you get in radios and long-distance calls... Now it makes sense, with the pale right on the doorstep."
"It sounds very much like entroponetic crosstalk. It happens sometimes when sending transmissions across long stretches of pale..."
"It was mathematical information -- from the anomaly -- presented as a waveform. That's what it was *technically* -- theoretically..." She shakes her head.

"It's a back-up of my former employer's project -- the radio game we were working on. It's stored on a *filament memory* just like the one inside this radiocomputer." She points to the glowing cube inside the machine.
"It's all around us," she waves her hand, "that's what 'on air' means."
"It's alright, lieutenant. He's simply cleaning the connections."
"It's completely ridiculous, but I believe we could transform the entire roundabout into one solid, *fractal antenna*."
"It's crosstalk. In all likelihood they can't hear you. You have to keep trying until we get a signal through."
"It's here."
"It's just me and my computer -- and it has been this way for weeks. Now please, give me some room. I need two seconds to see that you haven't destroyed anything."
"It's making a very *slight* difference. The signal is a bit clearer than it was."
"It's not working." The programmer removes her sweat-drenched headphones. "The crosstalk is simply too strong."

"It's quite common actually. When the signal gets routed through pale, all kinds of irregularities take place. You may hear snippets of someone else's conversation, or the voice of your former lover, or an echo of an event that took place 100 years ago."
"It's true, the drug fiends have made themselves quite comfortable. But *I* still have a great deal of work to do..."
"It's very likely, based on what we've recently learned. Give me a moment while I attempt to narrow the receiving mode..."
"Just 'messing with us'. Right. Well..."
"Just give me a second," she murmurs, "I'm almost..." She clocks up her typing speed.
"Just to be completely clear: I am here to conduct a citizen's investigation into a radio anomaly and I want nothing to do with the local vices of Martinaise. Got it? Thanks." She turns back to work.
"Just to be completely clear: I am here to conduct a citizen's investigation into a radio anomaly and I want nothing to do with the local vices of Martinaise. Okay? Thanks."
"Just walk over to the circle and follow my instructions: Move the third bowl two centimetres to the left and the fourth bowl five centimetres to the right. This should do the trick."
"Keep trying, officer. We'll get a signal through eventually."
"Let me know how it goes!"
"Like it would have made a difference -- the off-site copy was perfectly safe when the data loss happened. That data loss was *anomalous*." She crosses her arms defiantly.
"Lintel was able to divine the location of the anomaly from this broken copy. I want to repeat their calculation, only this time with better equipment."
"Maybe I'd have to be *on drugs* to get it, but to a sober mind it just sounds like uninspired rug whipping. No idea what it has to do with either dancing or music."
"Maybe, but..."
"Maybe. But it's oddly close to the physical coordinates of the data loss that led me to this place."
"Maybe." She rubs her face. "Maybe I'm just tired."
"Mhmh."
"Most of them were burnt down during the Revolution, or re-purposed before, during the Suzerain. I'm not saying *all* of them have one in them, but.."
"Mute disengaged." She lifts her hand from the keyboard. Complete silence fills the room.
"My intention is to run a power cable from the engine up to the antenna. It won't last forever, but it should give us enough time to establish a connection with Coalition Warship Archer."
"Never mind then, let's get on with our project... I am going to unmute the speakers on a count of five. Everyone ready?" She looks around the church.
"No one asked you to do anything *interesting* with my radiocomputer." She barely looks up from the keyboard. You hear the machine whir back to life.
"No one's hiding here." She barely looks up from the keyboard. You hear the machine whir back to life.
"No!" She looks up, disturbed. "No, of course not. I know a friend of a friend who used to freelance for the Coalition. I bought it from her."
"No, I don't."
"No, I'm not, it's just me and the..." She looks up at the ceiling before murmuring: "...*the crab-man*. I'm just doing some research. That's all."
"No, I'm not, it's just me and the..." She looks up at the ceiling without finishing her sentence. "I'm just doing some research. That's all."
"No, but you see, it doesn't matter whether you care about it or not. It's the law," she explains to you without even sparing a look, "I'm not going anywhere."
"No, certainly not. I've got a citizen's investigation to run and I want nothing to do with local vices."
"No, my hypothesis was wrong. According to this, I should have *heard* something if I got the coordinates right. Like I said: silence is only what surrounds it."
"No, of course not," she says, clearly disappointed. "Nothing happened, let's move on."
"No, of course not." She turns her tired, sardonic eyes to face you. "I feel even worse about drugs than I feel about nightclubs."
"No, officer, I don't *agree* to anything."
"No, that's not it."
"No, that's the production schedule you stole and accessed without authorization." She's tapping the table in a badly concealed impatience. "I don't need it."
"No, that's the production schedule, I don't need it. The right filament memory has 'OFF-SITE COPY' written on silver tape."
"No, we could not. This church is made from wood. I am not sure you understand how radios work."
"No, we should definitely do this. I *am* going to do this. Ready?" She pauses, looking around the church -- everyone stares at her hand on the keyboard.
"No, what they *really* should do is shut down the discomen for disturbing neighbourhood peace."
"No, you just printed out my personal log and wasted some paper." It does not look like a big loss to her.
"No, you're right, I'm not..." Her voice trails off, as she bends over to tinker with the machine's printer.
"No..." She breathes in, determined. "We *have* to do it." She puts on her oversized headphones, ready to press UNMUTE on the keyboard...
"No." She rests her face on her hands, massaging the forehead.
"No." She stares at you with droopy eyes. "She literally started praying for the higher powers when she first saw my Rehm Civic. I'm not making this up."
"No."
"Nope, not interested in your degenerate money schemes."
"North of here. Follow the coastline. I do not know how to explain it more simply."
"Not ghosts, officer. Crosstalk. You have to keep trying until we get a signal through."
"Not the most advanced model." She turns a few dials and then sets the transceiver aside. "But at least everything appears to be in order. Yes, this should serve our purposes."
"Not the sort of antenna we require. The Coalition has a near-monopoly on mega-low-frequency radio equipment. Fortunately, they do not have a monopoly on physics."
"Now I'm going to print it out to see what's left of it." She's already inserted the filament into the radiocomputer's core, ready to close the door.
"Now please, give me some room. I need two seconds to see that you haven't destroyed anything."
"Now you'll excuse me. I have to get back to my own work."
